## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Chavakajātaka* (Ja 309) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to its opening frame, the Buddha narrated the story while residing at Jetavana regarding the group of six monks (the *chabbaggiya*), who were reported to teach the Dhamma seated on a low seat to listeners occupying higher seats [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The Jātaka itself gives only an abbreviated summary of this present occasion (*paccuppannavatthu*) and explicitly refers the audience to the Vinaya for the full account [Appleton 2010; Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was born as an outcaste (*caṇḍālaputta* or *chavaka*, corresponding to Sanskrit *śvapaka*/*śvapaca*) who instructed a king after insisting on the proper decorum of sitting higher than the pupil [Appleton 2010; Cousins et al. 1974; Fausböll 1883; Silk]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the king as Ānanda and the outcaste youth as himself [Fausböll 1883].

Scholars note that the narrative directly parallels and amplifies the background account to the Vinaya training rule found in the Suttavibhaṅga (*Sekhiya* 69), which forbids a monk from teaching the Dhamma from a lower seat to someone sitting on a higher seat [Appleton 2010; Chakravarti 1996]. While the Jātaka fully establishes the narrative as a previous birth story, the Vinaya version only implies the Bodhisatta's identity and is not formally designated as a jātaka [Appleton 2010]. Uma Chakravarti also observes that the story illustrates social attitudes and ideological tensions between brāhmaṇas and renunciants, emphasizing the instruction to go forth as a wanderer [Chakravarti 1996].

 DharmaNexus confirms substantial Pali-internal text reuse between the *Chavakajātaka* and the *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga* (*Sekhiya* 69), as well as with commentary and subcommentary literature, notably the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Pācittiya-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā* [DharmaNexus].
